title: Salir vs Irse vs Dejar: How to Say “Leave” in Spanish
seo_title: Salir vs Irse vs Dejar: How to Say “Leave” in Spanish
meta_description: Salir vs irse vs dejar: three ways to say leave in Spanish. When to use each, going out and dating with salir, common mistakes, examples and a quick quiz.
excerpt: Leaving a place, leaving for good or leaving something behind: three verbs, one clear system.

body_html:
Salir vs irse is a pair that confuses learners because both can translate as “to leave”. Add dejar and you have three verbs for one English word. The system is logical: salir focuses on going out of a place, irse focuses on departing or going away, and dejar means leaving something or someone behind. Here’s how to choose, with plenty of real examples.

Quick answer
  • Salir (de) = to go out, exit, leave a place: Salgo de casa a las ocho.
  • Irse = to leave, go away (focus on departure): Me voy.
  • Dejar = to leave something or someone behind: Dejé las llaves.
  • Salir con also means to go out with or date someone.
{{toc}}

Salir vs irse vs dejar at a glance

VerbFocusExample
salirExiting a place, going outSalió de la oficina a las seis. She left the office at six.
irseDeparting, going awayYa se fue. He’s already gone.
dejarLeaving something or someoneDejó el carro en el garaje. He left the car in the garage.

Salir: going out of a place

Salir is about the act of exiting. It often takes de + the place you leave: salir de casa, salir del trabajo. The RAE dictionary defines it as passing from inside to outside.

  • ¿A qué hora sales del trabajo? What time do you finish work?
  • El tren sale a las 9:15. The train leaves at 9:15.
  • Salimos a cenar. We’re going out for dinner.
  • Sal de ahí. Get out of there.

Salir con: going out and dating

Salir con alguien means to go out with someone, often romantically: Estoy saliendo con alguien. (I’m seeing someone.) I cover dating vocabulary in {{link:first-date-in-spanish|first date in Spanish}}.

Irse: going away

Irse emphasizes leaving where you are, without necessarily naming the place:

  • Me voy, que es tarde. I’m off, it’s late.
  • ¿Ya te vas? Are you leaving already?
  • Se fueron a Chile. They moved / went away to Chile.
  • ¡Vete! Go away!

Compare: Voy a la playa (I’m going to the beach, destination) vs Me voy a la playa (I’m off to the beach, emphasis on leaving now).

{{image:2}}

Dejar: leaving something behind

  • Dejé el celular en el taxi. I left my phone in the taxi.
  • Deja la puerta abierta. Leave the door open.
  • Lo dejó su novia. His girlfriend left him.
  • Dejó su trabajo. She quit her job.

Dejar also means “to let”: Déjame pasar (Let me through), and dejar de + infinitive means “to stop”: Dejé de fumar (I stopped smoking).

{{book:the-mind-lies}}

Conjugation note

Salir is irregular in the first person present and in commands: salgo, sales, sale; command sal; future saldré. Irse uses the irregular ir: me voy, te vas, se va; past me fui; command vete. Dejar is regular.

Real conversations

At a party

  • A: ¿Ya te vas? ¡Si es temprano! (You’re leaving already? It’s early!)
  • B: Sí, mañana salgo de viaje a las seis. (Yes, tomorrow I’m leaving on a trip at six.)
  • A: Bueno, no dejes tu chamarra. (Okay, don’t leave your jacket.)

At work

  • A: ¿Dónde está Carlos? (Where’s Carlos?)
  • B: Se fue hace diez minutos. Salió con prisa y dejó la computadora prendida. (He left ten minutes ago. He rushed out and left his computer on.)

Common mistakes

IncorrectCorrectWhy
Salí mis llaves en casa.Dejé mis llaves en casa.Leaving an object is dejar
Dejo la oficina a las seis. (daily)Salgo de la oficina a las seis.Dejar + place can sound like quitting
Voy ahora. (meaning “I’m leaving now”)Me voy ahora.Departure needs irse
Salgo la casa.Salgo de casa.Salir needs de
{{image:3}}

A quick mental shortcut

Ask yourself one question: what am I leaving? If the answer is a building or room you walk out of, use salir. If you are simply announcing that you are going away from the people or the scene, use irse. If the thing you leave is an object, a job, a habit or a person you stop being with, use dejar. For example, at the end of a dinner you might say Bueno, me voy to your friends, then salgo del restaurante, and realize outside that dejé la bufanda en la silla. Three moments, three verbs.

Try it yourself

  1. I’m leaving, see you tomorrow. (Me voy, hasta mañana.)
  2. The plane leaves at noon. (El avión sale a mediodía.)
  3. I left my umbrella at the restaurant. (Dejé el paraguas en el restaurante.)
  4. Are you going out tonight? (¿Sales esta noche?)
  5. She’s been dating Marcos for a year. (Sale con Marcos desde hace un año.)

Movement verbs depend on perspective; for another example see {{link:ir-vs-venir|ir vs venir}}. For the full list of pairs, see {{link:spanish-confusing-words|my complete list of Spanish confusing words}}.

{{quiz}}

Final thoughts

Three verbs, three focuses: salir is going out of a place, irse is going away, dejar is leaving something behind. Ask yourself what you are leaving (a place, the scene or an object) and the right verb follows.

faq.q: What is the difference between salir and irse?
faq.a: Salir focuses on exiting a place (salir de casa), while irse focuses on departing or going away (me voy). Both can translate as “to leave”.

faq.q: How do you say “I left my keys” in Spanish?
faq.a: Dejé mis llaves. Leaving an object somewhere uses dejar, not salir.

faq.q: What does salir con alguien mean?
faq.a: It means to go out with someone, often romantically: Estoy saliendo con alguien (I’m seeing someone).
